items.title: 18.10.3 Reaction Between Copper(II) Ion and Iodide Ion

source_refs.note: Topic 18.10.3 with Quick Check 18.8, answered (PDF 34). The thiosulphate equation is added for the titration the book mentions. The exercises (PDF 35-37) are not part of the lesson body. Answers need review.

blocks.text: When excess potassium iodide is added to copper(II) sulphate solution, a white precipitate of copper(I) iodide forms in a red-brown solution of iodine: 2Cu2+(aq) + 4I-(aq) -> 2CuI(s) + I2(aq). The half-equations are:

The I2/I- couple has the higher E, so on these values alone it is iodine that should be reduced; the Cu2+/Cu+ couple has the lower E, which suggests Cu+ is a better reducing agent than I-. The calculated net standard potential for the reaction as written is negative. Yet the reaction goes forward, because the CuI formed keeps precipitating out of solution. This removes the Cu+ product and shifts the equilibrium to the right (Le Chatelier's principle).

blocks.title: Measuring the iodine
blocks.text: The amount of iodine formed can be measured by titration with a thiosulphate solution.
